title: Analysis of published accounts
overview: Ratio analysis converts financial-statement data into indicators of liquidity, profitability, efficiency, gearing and investor return. Calculation is only the first step: top answers compare, diagnose causes, explain consequences, propose actions and recognise limitations.
syllabusPoints: Calculate/interpret ROCE, gross profit margin and operating profit margin.
Calculate/interpret inventory turnover, receivables days and payables days.
Calculate/interpret P/E ratio, dividend yield and dividend cover.
Assess performance over time/against competitors and limitations of ratio analysis.

definitions.definition: Ability to meet short-term obligations when they fall due.
Ability to generate profit relative to revenue or capital employed.
How effectively working capital/assets are managed to support operations.
Extent to which long-term capital relies on non-current debt.
Operating profit generated as a percentage of capital employed.
Market price per share relative to earnings per share, often reflecting market expectations.

sections.title: Liquidity ratios
content: Current ratio compares current assets with current liabilities. Acid test removes inventory because it may be less liquid. Very low ratios can signal payment risk; very high ratios may signal inefficient working capital. Industry context matters.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content:
Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities
Acid test = (Current assets - Inventory) / Current liabilities

sections.title: Profitability ratios
content: Gross margin reflects selling price and direct cost of sales; operating margin also reflects operating expenses. ROCE relates operating profit to long-term capital committed.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content:
Gross profit margin = Gross profit / Revenue x100
Operating profit margin = Profit from operations / Revenue x100
ROCE = Profit from operations / Capital employed x100

sections.title: Efficiency ratios
content: Inventory turnover indicates how often inventory is sold/used. Receivables days estimates collection speed from credit customers; payables days estimates payment time to suppliers. Faster is not automatically better if it causes stockouts, customer loss or supplier conflict.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content:
Inventory turnover = Cost of sales / Average inventory
Receivables days = Trade receivables / Credit sales x365
Payables days = Trade payables / Credit purchases x365

sections.title: Gearing
content: Higher gearing means greater reliance on long-term debt and therefore more fixed interest/repayment risk. Debt can still improve owners' returns when operating returns exceed borrowing cost. Context includes cash-flow stability and interest rates.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content: Gearing (%) = Non-current liabilities / Capital employed x100

sections.title: Investor ratios
content: P/E indicates how highly the market values earnings; dividend yield compares cash dividend with market price; dividend cover indicates how many times profit covers the dividend and therefore how much safety/retention exists.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content:
P/E = Market price per share / Earnings per share
Dividend yield = Dividend per share / Market price per share x100
Dividend cover = Profit for the year / Annual dividend

sections.title: Interpreting and improving
content: Use previous years, targets, competitors or industry averages. Then move from result -> possible cause -> consequence -> action. Improvements may have trade-offs: tighter receivables collection improves cash but may reduce customer attractiveness.

sections.title: Limitations
content: Ratios rely on historical accounts and accounting policies, can be distorted by one-off items/inflation/window dressing, omit many intangibles and can be misleading across different business models. They identify symptoms, not proven causes.

formulas.label: Current ratio
formulas.note: Interpret using business model and trend, not a universal ideal.

formulas.label: Acid-test ratio
formulas.note: Removes the least liquid current asset.

formulas.label: Operating profit margin
formulas.note: Shows control of operating costs relative to sales.

formulas.label: ROCE
formulas.note: Compare with previous years, competitors and finance cost.

formulas.label: Gearing
formulas.note: Higher gearing generally increases financial risk.

analysisChains.title: Weak liquidity
steps: Current liabilities are high relative to liquid current assets
Operations can be disrupted despite reported profit
analysisChains.evaluation: A low ratio is not automatically bad: supermarkets can operate with low inventory days and strong, predictable cash sales.

examTips: Never call a ratio 'good' without a benchmark/context.
After calculation use: direction -> cause -> consequence -> possible action.
Use the Cambridge gearing formula: non-current liabilities / capital employed x100.
commonMistakes: Using revenue instead of credit sales/purchases where credit figures are provided.
Assuming lower inventory is always better.
Comparing unlike companies without industry/accounting context.
